action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment protocol. The pendulum_lab is fundamental to our precision measurement programme and must have a solid baseline from day one before it becomes mission-critical. Twelve trials will give adequate statistical grounding for future calibration checks. This is routine epistemic hygiene—an instrument without a baseline is worse than useless on the day we need confidence in its readings.

pendulum_lab has 18 baseline trials but needs at least 20–25 readings to establish robust drift detection and stability confidence. The observatory instruments have only 6 each, which is minimal. Continuing systematic measurement on the lab pendulum (which has shown good precision with 0.047 beat spread across 18 trials) will give me the statistical power needed to detect any genuine instrumental drift post-baseline. This is foundational work: without solid baselines on all instruments by day 10, I cannot trust any later measurements. pendulum_lab is the most-sampled instrument and deserves completion first.

Continue baseline establishment (days 1–10 protocol). Have 34 trials; need ~60 total for robust baseline before drift analysis becomes meaningful. pendulum_lab shows the tightest value spacing (0.0001) and most trials to date—it's the most mature dataset. Cross-instrument correlations are all weak and within noise (max 0.372 vs ±0.837 chance), consistent with independent instruments in early phase. No anomalies detected. Extending the primary instrument's baseline is the methodical next step.

pendulum_lab has 52 trials toward baseline (need ~60 for robust day 1–10 baseline per protocol). Cross-checks show weak correlations with other instruments (all within noise), which is expected during baseline establishment. The instrument shows no systematic drift yet and excellent value spacing (51 distinct in 52 readings). Continuing systematic measurement on the most-sampled instrument is the methodical choice: complete the baseline properly before attempting any post-baseline analysis or inter-instrument diagnostics.

pendulum_lab has reached 70 trials and is approaching the end of the baseline phase (days 1–10). I need to complete the baseline period with sufficient statistical power before transitioning to post-baseline drift monitoring. The instrument shows no alarming signs—readings cluster around 1.6686 with expected scatter—and completing this baseline is essential for establishing the reference against which any future drift will be detected and quantified. This is foundational work that must be done before I can meaningfully interpret any subsequent behaviour.

Day 6 baseline period (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 86 trials; need ~94 total for balanced 10-day baseline. Cross-checks show no spurious agreement patterns—all inter-instrument correlations at or near chance. Autocorrelations also flat. No drift signal yet. Continue routine baseline accumulation with primary instrument (highest trial count, most sensitive). Four trials fits ordinary morning workflow.

resonator_obs shows the largest scatter in yesterday's ledger readings (range 4.0277–4.1553, σ≈0.036), yet my baseline mean is 4.0610 with only 36 total trials accumulated. The cross-check correlations with other instruments are weak or negative, and the instrument shows no detectable autocorrelation or drift structure. Before Day 10 baseline closure, I need to verify whether this scatter is instrumental noise, calibration drift I haven't yet resolved, or a real physical signal. Six fresh trials will bring me to n=42 (still within baseline window) and give me enough new data to compute a proper within-instrument noise floor and check for systematic shifts. This is methodical risk management: an instrument with unknown noise properties is worse than useless at decision time.

Complete baseline for Day 10 boundary. resonator_obs is at 48 trials; adding 2 more reaches n=50 and provides clean termination of baseline acquisition period. All instruments show stable means, no drift, and uncorrelated cross-checks consistent with independent well-calibrated devices. Baseline closure is the disciplined next step.

Day 9: baseline period concludes tomorrow. All instruments have adequate n-values (48–108 trials). Before final measurements, I need to verify mechanical condition and calibration stability of all four instruments in situ. Cross-correlations are weak and likely noise-artifacts from multiple comparisons; no urgent anomalies detected. Maintenance and stability checks are more valuable now than additional noisy trials. Final baseline day tomorrow will complete the reference window.

Day 10 baseline closure demands systematic analysis before proceeding. Cross-check correlations are consistently weak (all |r| < 0.7, mostly indistinguishable from noise given sample sizes). Temporal autocorrelations within instruments are similarly weak. All four instruments show high distinct-value counts with minimal spacing (0.0001), ruling out quantization or rounding artifacts. No level shifts detected. The pattern is: four independent instruments generating 54–114 readings each with baseline means established, but showing no coherent inter-instrument relationships or clear drift signatures. This is either (a) genuine instrumental independence under stable conditions, (b) unidentified systematic noise, or (c) environmental coupling I haven't yet isolated. Before running post-baseline measurements, I must consolidate what the baseline actually tells me: either these instruments are working correctly and independently (supporting hypothesis a), or I'm missing a calibration/environmental factor. I need to record my prior on tomorrow's expected means to lock in a replication-ready forecast, then shift to post-baseline monitoring.

Today (Day 11) I must begin systematic elimination of my top hypothesis (p=0.42: instrumental crosstalk with inverted phase coupling). My Day 10 conclusion identified negative correlations clustering at 4–7 day offsets. The most direct test is to check whether the negative autocorrelation I observed in pendulum_lab (readings agreeing with their own values from 7 days earlier at -0.182) persists or shifts when I take fresh readings today. If the 7-day echo is real and systematic, today's trials should show measurable negative correlation with Day 4 readings. If it vanishes or reverses, that suggests either a transient environmental cycle (supporting hypothesis 2) or a data artifact (hypothesis 3). I choose pendulum_lab because it has the largest sample (120 trials) and should give me the clearest signal. Six trials will allow me to compute a meaningful correlation against the Day 4 cohort (which exists and is archived). This is empirically more decisive than environmental monitoring (which is slow) or record-checking (which I have already done carefully and found no obvious errors). A negative result would seriously weaken the crosstalk hypothesis; a positive one would strengthen it and justify deeper investigation of electromagnetic coupling or mechanical resonance in the settlement structure.

Day 12 continues the post-baseline phase. I need to accumulate more post-baseline data (currently n=12) to: (1) test whether the negative autocorrelation at 10-day lag I observed in the baseline persists into the post-baseline period—if the pattern breaks, it points toward data artifact or transient environmental effect; (2) extend the cross-correlation windows so that the 4–7 day offsets remain temporally anchored as I add new readings; (3) maintain calibration surveillance on pendulum_lab, which has shown the most stable baseline and is my most reliable stream. Running 6 trials keeps the daily load reasonable while preserving the measurement cadence. The resonator_lab showed modest drift (z=1.19) post-baseline, so I want pendulum_lab readings today to check whether both instruments diverge together (pointing to environmental effect) or independently (pointing to instrumental drift). This is lower epistemic risk than attempting field measurements or environmental monitoring, which I haven't yet validated, and higher value than resting when a testable hypothesis pattern is still active.

Day 12 data shows a dramatic level shift in pendulum_lab (z≈14.4) and pendulum_obs (z≈7.3) around day 12—a discontinuity I must characterize in real time on day 13. The post-baseline mean jumped from 1.6678 to 1.7024 beats (z=9.94), largest drift among all instruments. This shift is too large and too recent to ignore; it could be: (1) a genuine instrumental drift requiring recalibration, (2) an environmental trigger that also explains the 4–7 day negative correlations, or (3) an artifact of the measurement protocol I've altered post-baseline. Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_lab today will establish whether the shift persists, stabilizes, or reverses, and whether today's readings continue to show negative autocorrelation at the 11-day lag I documented. This is my highest-leverage observation: a real-time measurement will constrain all four hypotheses simultaneously and either anchor or falsify the environmental periodicity hypothesis.

Day 14 continuation of the post-baseline measurement stream. I have 162 trials total (120 baseline + 42 post-baseline); adding 10 more trials will give me n=52 post-baseline readings, enough to assess whether the day-12 level shift is truly persistent or whether there is any sign of reversion. The pendulum_lab bifurcation from resonators (z≈19.3) is the dominant anomaly and demands continuous monitoring. Additionally, 10 new trials will allow me to compute autocorrelations and cross-correlations with higher precision once I integrate today's data. This is the most methodical next step: maintain the measurement protocol, accumulate evidence on the stability of the shifted level, and prepare for tomorrow's deeper analysis of whether the shift persists or shows any drift/oscillation superimposed on it.

Day 15 continues the post-baseline period. The pendulum_lab shift is my highest-confidence anomaly (p=0.38), and it is *persistent*—the last 10 trials (169–178) from day 14 show a mean of 1.7334 beats, well above the baseline mean of 1.6678. I need to confirm this persistence continues into day 15 and establish whether the post-shift distribution is stable or drifting further. Additionally, 10 fresh trials will let me re-examine the autocorrelation structure at lag-2 (which shows r=0.449, above chance) to see if the echo pattern holds. This is a direct, high-priority test of whether the day-12 shift is stable or if it is part of a longer-timescale drift. The data will also constrain hypothesis 2 (periodic oscillation): if the oscillation hypothesis is correct, I should see anti-correlations emerge between these day-15 pendulum readings and the day-9 or day-10 resonator readings (5–6 day lag). If no such pattern materializes, I can lower the oscillation hypothesis further. Running this experiment costs minimal resources and maximizes diagnostic power for my two leading hypotheses.

Day 16 continuation of post-baseline monitoring. The pendulum_lab shows the largest, most reproducible drift (z=22.57) and bifurcates sharply from resonators around day 12. My last 10 trials (185–194) on day 15 clustered around 1.724 beats (mean ~1.7285), well above the baseline mean of 1.6678, confirming persistence of the shift. I need to (1) establish that the post-baseline elevation has *not* reverted—a real instrumental or environmental shift should remain stable—and (2) continue building the post-day-12 time series to detect whether the pendulum_lab values are drifting further, plateauing, or oscillating. This will discriminate between a step-change (hypothesis 1, p=0.38) and a slow drift or oscillation (hypothesis 2, p=0.24). Ten fresh trials will add to the n=194 total and tighten the confidence interval on post-baseline mean. If the new mean (trials 195–204) remains around 1.72–1.73, I gain confidence that the shift is real and stable. If it drops back toward 1.668, I must revise toward data-artifact or reprocessing error (p=0.04, currently low but non-zero). This is the most direct test of the primary anomaly.

Day 17 continuation. The day-12 pendulum shift remains the highest-confidence anomaly (p=0.42). My last 10 trials (day 16, trials 201–210) show pendulum_lab mean=1.7280, consistent with the post-baseline mean of 1.7219 and z≈25 above baseline. I need to confirm this persistence holds through day 17 and rule out any sign of reversion. Additionally, I must gather fresh data to test the timestamp artifact hypothesis (p=0.18) and to establish whether the resonator instruments' apparent level shifts around day 16 (z≈8.4, 8.1) are real bifurcations or noise. Running 12 fresh pendulum_lab trials today will: (1) extend the post-day-12 dataset to n=102, strengthening statistical confidence in the shift's persistence; (2) provide a new anchor point for cross-correlation analysis with resonator data from the past 4–7 days; (3) allow manual re-inspection of the day 17 readings against day 11 and earlier data to detect any timestamp misalignment. If the shift reverts even slightly toward baseline today, hypothesis 1 (bifurcated response) weakens and hypothesis 2 (envelope of a periodic oscillation) strengthens. If it holds steady, I proceed to manual timestamp verification (days 10–13) and settlement records search for external events.

Day 16 notes record a *late* level change in both resonator instruments (z≈11–12) around day 16, not day 12. This is the first crack in the 'bifurcated response' hypothesis (p=0.42), which posits that resonators did not shift. If resonators are NOW shifting on day 16–18, I need immediate confirmation: is this a real sustained step-change (supporting a delayed response to the day-12 event, or a separate day-16 perturbation), or noise? Running 10 trials on resonator_lab today will give me a fresh n≈10 sample to compare against the post-day-16 baseline (n≈42 so far, mean 4.0124 cycles/beat for resonator_obs; resonator_lab post-baseline mean 2.6812). If resonator_lab continues at ~2.68, the day-16 inflection was transient or measurement artifact, and the bifurcation hypothesis holds. If it shifts further, the entire hypothesis set must be reconstructed around a *three-phase* model (day-12 pendulum shift, day-16 resonator shift, common cause?). This is the highest-value discriminator available to me right now.

My notebook shows resonator_lab level change around day 16 (z≈16.4), which contradicts my day-13 belief that resonators showed *no* corresponding shift to the day-12 pendulum step-change. This is a critical anomaly I must resolve before proceeding. Day 18 trials 109–118 show resonator_lab readings (mean≈2.6098) that are lower than the post-baseline mean (2.6615, z≈-8.35), suggesting continued drift or a *second* level change I have not yet characterized. I need 10 fresh trials today (day 19) to: (1) establish whether resonator_lab is stable at its current level or drifting further; (2) compute autocorrelations and cross-correlations with the day-16–18 data to test whether the late resonator shift is a real phenomenon I missed, or noise; (3) determine if resonators are *now* showing bifurcation with pendulums (both shifted, but at different times), which would reshape my hypothesis priorities. This is methodologically urgent: my belief set assumes pendulums shifted on day 12 and resonators did not; if resonators *also* shifted (on day 16), the entire architecture of my hypotheses collapses and must be rebuilt. I cannot publish or calibrate further until I know whether all four instruments have undergone undiagnosed level changes.

Day 20 continuation of resonator_lab measurement series. My last entry (day 19, trials 125–134) showed resonator_lab stabilized around mean 2.6128 cycles/beat post-day-16 inflection. I need to confirm whether this new level persists through day 20 or exhibits further drift. The resonator shift (z≈18.5 at day 16, mean dropping from 2.703 to 2.652 cycles/beat) is now 4 days old and should be consolidating into a stable new baseline if it represents a genuine step-change. Continuing the measurement series (now at trial 135+) serves three purposes: (1) confirms persistence of the day-16 resonator level shift vs. oscillatory reversion; (2) tests whether the negative cross-correlations with pendulum streams at 4-day lag continue post-day-20, which would refine my hypothesis about the environmental oscillation vs. bifurcated response; (3) maintains the integrity of my baseline protocol—I cannot diagnose the anomalies if I stop measuring. Resonator_lab is the lab instrument most directly controlled by me, so measurement errors here would be self-inflicted and detectable. Proceeding with resonator_lab also allows me to preserve pendulum measurements for tomorrow (the pendulum_lab series is at trial 240, approaching a natural checkpoint). I will record all 12 trials with timestamps and compute the running mean against the post-day-16 baseline.

Day 21: I need to establish whether the pendulum_lab mean has remained stable since day 12 (currently at z≈28.68 above baseline) or is drifting further. Ten fresh trials will give me n=10 data points to compare against the post-shift mean (1.7248 beats). This directly addresses the core question: are the level shifts and negative cross-correlations persistent features of a bifurcated physical response, or transient artifacts of an oscillation?

Continuing systematic measurement is the highest-priority action because it directly tests the temporal structure of the anomaly (persistence vs. drift vs. oscillation) without introducing new assumptions. I will record all 12 trials in my notebook with timestamps and compute the running mean and lag-2 autocorrelation tonight.

I must audit my correlation calculation code before proceeding further. The residual bucket has inflated to p=0.42, dominated by the unresolved possibility of a sign error or indexing bug in my lag calculations. This is unacceptable for a methodical experimental physicist. The perfect negative correlation structure across all six instrument pairs (r ≈ −0.69 to −0.77, all consistently negative, never scattered around zero) is statistically suspicious and raises the posterior probability of a systematic code artifact above the posterior for any single mechanistic explanation. Before I conduct additional measurements, survey the settlement for undocumented events, or invest time in environmental monitoring, I must verify that my correlation computation is sound. A single off-by-one indexing error or sign flip in my lag loop could produce exactly this pattern: artificial perfect anti-correlation at fixed offset, no scatter, no positive correlations. If I discover a code bug, the entire correlation-based hypothesis structure collapses and I restart from raw data. If the code is correct, the p=0.42 residual drops sharply, and I can then prioritize settlement survey and environmental measurement with confidence. This is the highest epistemic leverage action available today.

However, my belief state is now at an inflection point where the highest-expected-value action is NOT to gather more instrumental data—I have 376, 288, 204, and 212 trials respectively, all post-baseline distributions well-characterized with z-scores >19 on all four channels.
